sentences.text: Plumadraco was a medium-sized enantiornithine bird belonging to the family Bohaiornithidae.
Its body mass is estimated to fall between 112 and 144 grams.
Feathers are preserved on both the wings and the tail, including a pair of extremely elongated tail feathers that are about twice the length of the animal’s body.
These tail feathers terminate in distinctive racket-like structures at their tips.
The holotype preserves soft tissues, providing an unusually complete view of its plumage.
The elongated tail plumes are among the longest known for early Cretaceous birds.
Plumadraco was discovered in China within the Jiufotang Formation, which dates to the Aptian age of the Early Cretaceous.
The species was described by Clark and colleagues, and the holotype specimen (accession STM11-4) is curated at the Shandong Tianyu Museum of Nature.
The unusually long tail feathers are interpreted as display structures used in courtship rituals.
The authors infer that the specimen likely represents a male, based on the presumed sexual dimorphism of such ornamental feathers.
Phylogenetic analysis recovers it as the sister taxon to an unnamed immature bohaiornithid (CUGB-P1202) within a group that also contains Sulcavis.
The Jiufotang Formation, where Plumadraco lived, represents lake-margin environments of the Early Cretaceous Aptian.
Because soft-tissue preservation is limited for most enantiornithines, it remains challenging to pinpoint the exact selective pressures that drove the evolution of ornamental feathers in this group.
